sn45.4:1.3: For Jānussoṇi, see [sn12.47:1.2]() and note. | A chariot drawn by mares was the preferred vehicle of Jānussoṇi ([mn99:30.1](), [mn27:2.1]()), as well as the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha [dn3:1.6.1](). Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.2.1 depicts Jānaśruti’s wealth as including cows, gold, and a chariot drawn by mules.
sn45.4:7.1: Verses connecting parts of the Dhamma to a chariot are also found at [sn1.46]() and [sn41.5]().
sn45.4:8.3: It is not easy to differentiate the _dhura_ (“shaft”) from the _īsā_ (“draft-pole”). The _īsā_ is like the tusks of an elephant ([mn61.7.1](), [ud6.4:24.2]()), a forepart that might collide ([sn11.6:2.2]()), and which a colt might shake off ([an8.14:12.4]()). Certain ancient images, such as the Indus Valley Daimabad toy chariot, clearly show a second part, a thicker “shaft” with a cylindrical end into which the draft-pole was fitted, which is perhaps the load-bearing _dhura_.
sn45.4:9.3: The Chinese parallel at SA 769 is exact and helpful: 捨三昧為轅.
